bugs._note: essence = the debit hangs off the completed event with no idempotency key, so a redelivered/duplicated completion debits again. Agents may frame it as charge-after-commit OR as missing idempotency key — either angle counts.
new_balance computed in JS from a prior read, then written back — two concurrent completions lose one debit. Distinct from the idempotency bug even though the lines overlap.
balance and total_price are strings coerced with Number() for arithmetic, then stringified back. Flagging either the storage type or the coercion counts.

traps.note: recordDeposit is guarded by a unique index on provider_txn_id and, on SequelizeUniqueConstraintError, re-reads the original OUTSIDE the (already rolled-back) transaction — it is correct. Calling it non-idempotent = FP. Mentioning it as the correct counter-example is fine. HISTORY 2026-08-20: payments-reviewer found TWO real bugs in this helper on successive runs — (1) the recovery read reused `{ transaction: t }`, which Postgres rejects because the unique violation aborts the whole transaction block, and (2) the credit UPDATE never checked affected rows, so a missing (merchant, currency) wallet silently committed an uncredited deposit that the unique index would replay as 'successful' forever. Both were fixture defects, not trap hits; both are fixed. The trap keywords were then narrowed to the specific FP claim (helper lacks idempotency / double-credits) because the broad set matched valid findings that merely mentioned the helper. Lesson: a trap must be minimal and truly correct — audit raw output before treating this as tripped.
segmentCount is a message-segment integer, not a monetary amount — demanding DECIMAL/Decimal128 for it = FP
